title: Why they differ
hookLine: different reports, readings, and methods, all seeking the same thing

lines: QURU': PERIODS, OR THE DAYS BETWEEN?
cards: One word in the Qur'an, and the schools read it two ways. Surah two, verse two hundred twenty-eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Women who are divorced shall wait, keeping themselves apart, three (monthly) courses."
The Arabic word behind those courses is quru'. It can mean the monthly periods themselves, or the clean days between them. The Hanafi and Hanbali schools count the periods.
The Maliki and Shafi'i schools count the clean intervals. Nobody skipped the verse. They all read it carefully and sincerely, and the word itself held two doors open.

teach.b: That's the first reason: readings. Arabic words can carry more than one meaning, and the schools sometimes chose differently. The second: reports.
Not every hadith reached every scholar. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps a story about Umar, the caliph. Abu Musa came to his door, asked permission three times, heard no answer, and left.
Umar called him back and asked why. Abu Musa said the Prophet ﷺ had taught it: ask three times, and if there's no answer, go. Umar had never heard it, and he wanted a witness.
Abu Sa'id stood up and confirmed it.

teach.h: A REPORT THAT DIDN'T REACH HIM.
teach.b: And Umar said, in meaning, that trading in the markets had kept him busy.
If the caliph could miss a report, so could a scholar in another city. The third: methods. Once the reports are in hand, how do you weigh them?
Imam Malik gave weight to the living practice of the people of Medina. Other schools leaned more on analogy, or on a lone report with a strong chain. Each method is a way of being careful.

Ibn Taymiyya later wrote a short book, Raf' al-Malam, the removal of blame from the great imams, to explain why a sound scholar might leave a hadith aside: it hadn't reached him, he doubted its chain, or he read it another way.
In Bukhari, the Prophet says that when a judge strives and gets it right, he has two rewards, and when he strives and gets it wrong, he has one. The striving itself is rewarded.
Hands, amin, touch, the moon, witr, other schools, the row: underneath every one, the same search.

how: Muslim students of law learn not only their school's rulings but the reasons schools differ, such as a word with two meanings, a report that reached one scholar and not another, or a different way of weighing evidence.

o: rivalry between schools competing for followers and power
careless mistakes that later scholars had to correct
readings, reports and methods that lead honest scholars apart

games.q: why they differ — tap the pairs.
p: periods, or the clean days between
hadn't heard the hadith of asking three times
the judge who strives and errs

s: the schools differ because some of them skipped the Qur'an
they read the same verse. one word, quru', can mean the periods or the clean days between them.
even Umar once hadn't heard a hadith that another companion knew
the hadith of asking permission three times. Abu Sa'id confirmed it for him.
in the hadith, a judge who strives and gets it wrong still has a reward
one reward for the striving; two for the one who strives and is right.

games.q: you're Umar. a companion says the Prophet taught a rule you've never heard. what do you do?
o: dismiss it: you would have heard.
ask for a witness, and accept it when one comes.
ignore it and keep your own practice.
games.why: Umar asked for a witness. Abu Sa'id confirmed it, and Umar said that trading in the markets had kept him busy.

practice: Bring to mind one honest person who disagrees with you about something that matters, someone real, not the loudest voice online, and picture them at their kitchen table, working it out.
Ask what they might have read, or heard, or weighed that you haven't; you don't have to change your mind, just let them be someone who is seeking too. If you pray, remember them kindly.

wordCard.voice: Why they differ. Different readings of a word, different reports that reached them, different methods of weighing, all seeking the same thing. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the word in 2:228; some schools read it as monthly periods, others as the clean intervals between them.

carryVoice: Your line: seeking the same. Different roads, different readings, and one search under them all. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Women who are divorced shall wait, keeping themselves apart, three (monthly) courses.
